summary: Thailand lies in the middle of the Indochinese Peninsula and is the only country in Southeast Asia never colonized by Europeans; it is known for its Buddhist temples, food and tourism, and is a constitutional monarchy.

ranking.name: Theravada Buddhism
ranking.description: In the 13th century King Ramkhamhaeng of the Sukhothai Kingdom invited Theravada monks from Nakhon Si Thammarat in the south, who followed the Sri Lankan tradition, to spread the teaching, and from then on Theravada Buddhism became the state religion of the Thai kingdoms. Through the Ayutthaya dynasty and the Chakri dynasty from 1782, the king has always been the supreme patron of Buddhism, and in the 19th century Rama IV (Mongkut) even founded the Dhammayut order to push reform of the monastic community. Because Buddhism, the nation and the monarchy form a trinity, and with the custom of men briefly ordaining as monks and temple education, the great majority of Thais follow Theravada Buddhism.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Muslims are mainly the Malays of the three southern provinces of Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat. The area was originally the Sultanate of Pattani, was Islamized from about the 15th century, and was formally incorporated into Siam after the 1909 Anglo-Siamese Treaty. Because the language and religion differ from the Thais, and assimilation policies provoked resentment, the southern conflict flared up again from 2004. In addition, Bangkok also has Muslim descendants of Persian traders from the Ayutthaya period, of the Cham and others.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Catholic missionaries came to Siam in the 17th century with French envoys during the reign of King Narai of Ayutthaya, and in the 19th century American Protestant missionaries brought Western medicine and printing. But because Buddhism is so closely tied to national identity, there have always been few converts; since the 20th century Christianity has spread mainly among minorities such as the Karen in the northern mountains, so its share nationwide is very low.

religion.background: Thai Buddhism was established as the Theravada tradition in the 13th century under the Sukhothai Kingdom, and from then on the king, as patron of Buddhism, made Buddhism, the nation and the monarchy the three pillars of Thai identity. Buddhism has absorbed Brahmanical rituals and spirit beliefs, and the spirit houses commonly seen at the entrances of Thai homes are one example. The southern Pattani region, because it historically belonged to a Malay sultanate, is mainly Islamic, while Christianity was introduced from the 17th century but has had limited influence. The Thai constitution guarantees religious freedom, but Buddhism still enjoys a special position in society and politics.

ranking.name: Thai (Central Thai)
ranking.description: The Thai people moved south from southern China to the Chao Phraya basin about a thousand years ago, and the Thai alphabet appeared in the 13th century under the Sukhothai Kingdom. Central Thai was originally the dialect of Ayutthaya and the Bangkok area and became the standard language because the capital is located there; in the 1930s–40s the Phibun government pursued a "Thaification" nationalist policy, requiring the use of standard Thai in schools and government throughout the country. Today almost all Thais can speak Central Thai, but only about a third have it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Isan
ranking.description: Isan is the mother tongue of the inhabitants of the northeast (the Isan region) and is in fact a variety of Lao. The area historically belonged to the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang, and after King Anouvong's uprising in Laos failed in 1827, Siam moved large numbers of Lao people to the west bank of the Mekong; after the Franco-Siamese War of 1893 the Mekong became the border, and the Lao west of the river stayed in Thailand. The Bangkok government calls the region "Isan" (northeast), playing down Lao identity, and Isan is also written in the Thai script.

ranking.name: Northern Thai
ranking.description: Northern Thai, also called "Kham Mueang," is the language of the Lanna Kingdom, founded in 1292 by King Mangrai and centered on Chiang Mai, which originally used its own "Lanna script." Lanna was gradually incorporated into Siam from the end of the 19th century to the early 20th century, and standard Thai education replaced the Lanna script, but people in the north still use Northern Thai in daily life, and in recent years there has been a movement to revive the Lanna script.
ranking.greeting: สวัสดีเจ้า

ranking.name: Pattani Malay
ranking.description: Pattani Malay is the mother tongue of the Malay Muslims of the three southern provinces and derives from the time of the Pattani Sultanate, traditionally written in the Arabic-based "Jawi script." After incorporation into Siam in 1909, the government pursued a Thai-only education policy, which local people saw as assimilation pressure, and language has therefore become one of the core issues of southern ethnic identity and conflict.

language.history: Thai belongs to the Kra–Dai family; after the ancestors of the Thais moved south from southern China to the Indochinese Peninsula, the Thai alphabet, based on the Khmer script, developed in the 13th century under the Sukhothai Kingdom. In the Ayutthaya and Bangkok periods it absorbed a great deal of Pali, Sanskrit and Khmer vocabulary for religious and royal use. In the early 20th century the government pursued a national language policy that took the Central Thai of Bangkok as the national standard. Isan in the northeast, Northern Thai in the north and Pattani Malay in the south reflect the history of Thailand's incorporation of Lao, Lanna and Malay regions.

ranking.name: Tom yum goong
ranking.description: A hot-and-sour broth of lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves and chili, with fresh shrimp or seafood and straw mushrooms added, seasoned with fish sauce and lime juice, hot, sour and fragrant.
ranking.history: Tom yum originated in the central plains of the Chao Phraya basin, where there is a dense network of rivers and an abundance of shrimp and herbs. Chili peppers are native to the Americas and reached the Ayutthaya kingdom through Portuguese merchants from the 16th century, gradually becoming the soul of Thai cuisine. With the rise of Thai tourism and Thai restaurants abroad in the late 20th century, tom yum became one of the best-known Thai dishes in the world; in 2024 "Tom Yum Kung" was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: Pad Thai
ranking.description: Rice noodles stir-fried over high heat with shrimp, tofu, egg, bean sprouts and garlic chives, seasoned with tamarind paste, fish sauce and sugar, then sprinkled with crushed peanuts and a squeeze of lime juice.
ranking.history: Fried rice noodles were originally a noodle dish brought by Chinese immigrants; in the 1930s–1940s the Phibun government, pursuing a nationalist policy, strongly promoted this dish, named "Pad Thai," to reduce rice consumption and build national identity, encouraging vendors to sell it. The dish therefore carries traces of both Chinese food and Thai nationalism. Today it is Thailand's most representative street snack and also the signature dish of Thai restaurants abroad.

ranking.name: Som tam (green papaya salad)
ranking.description: Green papaya is shredded and pounded in a mortar with chili, garlic, tomato and long beans, then seasoned with fish sauce, lime juice and palm sugar, sour, spicy, sweet and salty.
ranking.history: The papaya is native to Central America and was brought to Southeast Asia by Spanish and Portuguese navigators after the 16th century. Green papaya salad originated with the Lao and the Isan region of northeastern Thailand and is traditionally eaten with sticky rice and grilled chicken. In the 1960s–1970s large numbers of Isan people went to work in Bangkok and brought this home dish to the capital, and it has since become one of the most common street foods throughout Thailand.

ranking.name: Green curry
ranking.localName: แกงเขียวหวาน (Kaeng khiao wan)
ranking.description: A green curry paste pounded from green chilies, lemongrass and galangal is simmered with coconut milk, with chicken or beef, Thai small eggplants and holy basil added, spicy with a touch of sweetness.
ranking.history: Thai curries are based on curry pastes pounded from fresh spices, unlike the Indian method using dried spice powders. Green curry took shape relatively late and is generally believed to have appeared in Thai recipe literature only around the early 20th century; "sweet green" refers to its green color and the sweetness from the coconut milk. It is common in both court and home cooking, eaten with white rice or rice noodles, and has become the best-known Thai curry internationally.

ranking.name: Mango sticky rice
ranking.localName: ข้าวเหนียวมะม่วง (Khao niao mamuang)
ranking.description: Sticky rice is steamed and mixed with coconut milk sweetened and salted, then served beside slices of ripe mango, topped with thick coconut milk and sprinkled with mung beans.
ranking.history: Sticky rice has been the traditional staple of northern and northeastern Thailand for thousands of years, and coconut-milk sweet sticky rice is a common dessert in the center. Mangoes are abundant every April–May, just in time for the Thai New Year Songkran water festival, so mango sticky rice has become a seasonal festival dessert. In 2022 the Thai rapper Milli ate mango sticky rice on the stage of the Coachella music festival in the United States, drawing worldwide attention and making it even better known internationally.
